journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first.

body: At half past noon the Anacapa waffle irons are going down the line like a drum corps that has never rehearsed, each one finishing on its own beep, and the tray belt by the dish window rattles forks away into the back of the building. Doug Pruitt has taken the end of the long table by the glass the way he takes everything, by opening a laptop on it.
Theo comes in last, still in the navy Sigma Rho blazer, with a banana and a glass of water on his tray. His breath reaches the table about a second ahead of him.

“Brooks Callahan,” he says, sitting, “handed me a raw onion at eight-twenty this morning. Not as a gesture. A yellow onion, skin on, in front of the entire lacrosse team, who stopped chewing.” He peels the banana. “Brooks says it builds character. I ate it like an apple, and it built breath.”

Kevin has divided his tray by macronutrient, chicken and egg and cottage cheese in a tidy triptych, and is explaining to Margot that thirty grams a meal is the number. She has not asked. “So the body,” Margot says, over a coffee she takes black as a position, “converts cottage cheese into opinions.”
“Basically,” Kevin says, cheerfully, and eats the egg.
“Dude,” Doug says, scrolling ESPN with one finger. “Pete Carroll is going to *Seattle*. It rains there, dude. It rains *on purpose*.”
“My father had lunch with him in November,” Theo says. “He ordered for him.”
Doug opens his mouth, looks at Theo’s face, and shuts it. The banana goes on being peeled.
“And McGwire,” Doug tries, recovering. “All those years, and now he’s *sorry*. He’s sorry he got caught.”
“He’s sorry in the passive voice,” Margot says.
“Mistakes were made,” says Theo, “by a younger, larger man.”
“Laney would’ve *loved* this,” Doug says. “Where’s Laney?”
“Laney has a mandatory Pi Lam luncheon,” Theo says. “Chicken salad. They take attendance by photograph.”
Margot looks at Theo. Theo looks at the banana.
Theo’s iPhone lights on his tray. He reads it without picking it up, and turns it face down beside the banana peel.
“Laney,” he says, “would like me to know that the chicken salad is excellent, and that she is sitting with people who understand what the Like button means.”

Doug works it out a beat behind everyone. “Dude. You *liked* it?” He scrolls up the wall to the status and finds it, and turns the laptop so the table can see the little blue thumb with the names after it. Theo Vance, first.
“I like a great many things, Pruitt. It’s a reflex. I liked the Pope in Cameroon.” Theo eats a piece of banana. “I have been informed it was not a reflex. I have been informed it was a position.”
Margot writes something in her notebook and doesn’t say what.

Doug swings the laptop toward Jack. “Okay. Okay okay okay. I have to do the wall.” Jack’s profile is open on it. Doug friended everyone on the fourth floor in September, and since nine this morning, by his own account, he has been reading Jack’s wall in the back of Psych 1 with the sound off. “I’m going to read it,” he says, “as a public service.”

body: “That was *forty minutes ago*,” Doug says, with something like awe. “Dude. You were in *class*.” He does Kayla Ruiz, whom none of them have met, as a girl whispering in a library. Jack has a hand flat on the table. In the picture, small, from below and at an angle, he is writing something in a margin and Skye is looking at him and not at Fenner.
“Is she coming to the Fishbowl again?” Doug asks, his own voice again, and sincere. “Tell her the foosball’s fixed.”
“It isn’t,” says Theo.
“It’s *mostly* fixed.”
“It has one goalie, Pruitt, and a rumor.”
“Log in, dude.” Doug logs himself out with a flourish and slides the laptop across the table. “You’ve got requests.”

Theo looks away toward the waffle line, like a gentleman at somebody else’s cash machine. Doug does not look away. Jack types his password with his shoulder between the keys and the table, and fools no one, and the home page comes up.

body: The requests run down the column in little gray thumbnails: St. Brigid’s, Mooney, the CYO gym, a girl from Poland (the Ohio one) who dated a guy who dated a friend of Gina’s. Of the six messages, one is from his eighth-grade CYO coach, in lowercase: *proud of you son*. One is from somebody’s mother, whom he cannot place at all: *Jack honey is she Catholic*.
Every one of them can see him now, all of Glenwood Avenue at once, and not one of them has ever heard that there is a girl in New Orleans.
“So what do you want to do, dude?” Doug says.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 5:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL → 5:40 PM · THE FISHBOWL
body: Kevin’s text finds him on the fourth-floor landing, where the east stairwell keeps its one good bar: *CNN in the Fishbowl. Come down.* The landing window has gone from gold to a deep blue since the last time he looked. Sunset was at three minutes past five, and the building didn’t announce it.
He is a flight and a half from the second floor when the voice comes up the well. It is Laney’s, and it is low, which it never is, and it carries anyway.
“…don’t you dare tell him, Theodore. Not one —”

On the ground floor the fire door bangs, a kid with a laundry bag shouldering in from the dusk, and the sentence stops where it is. Two faces tip up through the rail of the second-floor landing. Jack has one foot down on the next step and leaves it there.
“Costigan,” Theo says. The blazer, the tie, no hitch at all. “Laney was briefing me on rush etiquette.”

Laney, in the Pi Lam hoodie with the hood up, looks at Jack for one breath and goes through the second-floor door into her own hall without a word. Jack takes the last flight down. Theo falls in beside him on the stairs.
“Never write the thank-you note before they’ve bid,” Theo says. “It reads as presumption. The lacrosse team will talk to you about stationery for an hour. I have, in fact, been talked to.”
“Good to know,” Jack says.
“Pi Lam has forms for the forms,” Theo says. “It’s fascinating. Laney has a binder.”
“Laney has a binder?”
“In *tabs*, Costigan.” Theo’s tie is perfect, and has been since breakfast. “I’d show you, but it’s privileged.”

In the Fishbowl the television is on CNN with the sound up, and the room has arranged itself around it without anyone deciding to. It is night in New York, and the same hour in Port-au-Prince. The screen has a studio, a map with one dot on it, and under the anchor the same few pictures in rotation, because they are the pictures there are. A white building folded down on itself, floor on floor. A street full of dust with people standing in the middle of it, because the middle of the street is the one place nothing can come down on them. A woman on a curb in a blanket, holding a phone away from her face and looking at it.
“Dude,” Doug says, once, to the screen, and the *u* is one *u* long.

A correspondent says he has not been able to reach his own bureau since the afternoon. The lines are down. The anchor reads a statement from the White House, which says the President has been briefed and that help is being readied, and turns to a man from a relief agency and asks him how many. “I think we’re talking about thousands,” the man says, slowly, like somebody who is guessing and hates it. “We simply don’t know.”
“We don’t,” the anchor says. “Anybody who gives you a number tonight is guessing.”
Jack’s hand has gone to the medal under his shirt. It isn’t for anything. It is there.

Kevin is forward on the arm of the middle couch with his BlackBerry in both hands. Doug is standing; Jack has never seen him stand for a television program. Margot is in the armchair with her arms crossed and her Docs flat on the floor. Theo does not sit. He stands by the glass door in the blazer, since the Sigma Rho smoker is at six, with his eyes on the screen. In the doorway beside him Priya, crossing the lobby with her clipboard, has stopped with the pen up over the page. The pen doesn’t come down.
“Quiet hours are suspended in the Fishbowl until further notice,” she says, to the clipboard. “I don’t have a form for that. I’m going to make one.” And goes on across the lobby.

“It isn’t the building, a lot of the time,” Kevin says. He is looking at the BlackBerry, not the screen, and the sunny has gone out of him; what is left sounds like a very good student. “The ones they pull out on day three. They talk to you. They’re fine. The muscle’s been dying under the weight the whole time, and it’s holding everything it let go of, potassium mostly, and when you lift the weight it all goes to the heart at once. They can die in the ambulance.” He swallows. “It’s called crush syndrome. I did my science fair on it. Armenia, 1988.” Doug looks at him. “Second place,” Kevin says.
“It sounds like a good project,” Jack says.
“It was a tri-fold,” says Kevin, and the old Kevin is there for a syllable, and gone.
“How long can somebody last under there?” Theo says.
He says it to the television. Kevin answers it the same way.
“Days,” Kevin says. “If they’ve got air.”
On the screen the white building comes around again in the same still.

“I gave this afternoon,” Margot says, to the room. “Partners In Health. They have been in the Central Plateau since 1987, they have clinics standing and people in them who speak Kreyòl, and they don’t have to arrive. Give there. Not to the Red Cross. Not to the Church.”
“Catholic Relief is the Church,” Kevin says, not looking up. “And they’re in Haiti.”

“Then I amend it.” Margot uncrosses her arms. “Not to the Church, except the part that was already there and has been for years. That part I’ll allow. I am still giving to Farmer. Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. You’d like him. Lena would *love* him.”

She hears it. She stops with her mouth a little open, and uncaps her pen, and writes something small in the notebook on her knee, and shuts the notebook on the pen. Jack keeps his eyes on the building on the screen.
“I had a Haitian roommate,” Doug says, to the screen. “Ninth grade, at band camp. Pierre. His family’s in Delray. I don’t have his number. Why don’t I have his number?”
“Your mom will have his mom,” Kevin says.
“She’ll have his mom.” Doug says it like a lifeline, and has his phone out and is through the glass and across the lobby before the anchor has finished the sentence he was on.
Kevin’s BlackBerry buzzes in his hands, and he reads it out flat.

body: Theo’s iPhone lights in his hand. He reads the screen like a menu he already knows. “A press release,” he says, to no one in particular, “from my father’s office, forwarded by somebody who was told to forward it. *Meridian Pictures will commit* — no figure, I notice — *said Richard Vance, president of production.* Second paragraph. That’s where the money keeps its coat on.” He turns the phone face-down against his thigh and checks the Rolex. “Brooks has a list.”
He has his hand on the glass door.

choices.text: Go after him to the door. “You okay?”
response: Jack gets to the glass before it has finished swinging. “You okay?”
“It’s rush, Costigan. Everyone’s okay at rush.” Theo reaches up and straightens Jack’s collar, which doesn’t need it, and goes out into the dark with the phone still face-down in his hand.

response: “I’m not a knees person,” Theo says. He stands there with the door held open and the dusk coming in around him, and looks once more over his shoulder at the screen. “Light one for me. Whatever it is you light.”

choices.text: Watch the TV. Let him go.
response: Theo goes. Kevin watches him cross the lobby; Jack watches Kevin.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 11:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL COMPUTER
body: At twenty to midnight the Fishbowl has its lights off and the lobby comes through the glass. The beige tower in the corner past the foosball table is the building’s one public computer, under a sign in Priya’s hand: 20 MINUTES. THIS MEANS YOU. Through the glass Marcus is awake at the front desk with his orgo book closed, a thing Jack hasn’t seen, and the radio low on KCBX, where a woman from a relief organization says again that the phones are down and that she will say it again at the top of the hour.

Theo is not back from the smoker. Upstairs 412 has its lamp on and Theo’s half of it empty, and a closet door that won’t latch unless you lift it, and Jack has come down four flights to a beige computer instead. Today’s *Tide* is on the coffee table with a story about parking on the front, printed before any of it. The keys are sticky. He logs in as himself, and the lobby watches him do it, and his own wall comes up first.

body.text: Ryan has answered under his comment, in capitals: HI JACK. GLENWOOD AVE SAYS HI BACK. Four more people have said hi under that.
Tommy’s repost is at the top of his wall with nineteen comments, most of them *lol*.
There are two more requests since lunch. He accepts those too.
There are twenty-six friend requests now. He doesn’t open them.

body: Kayla Ruiz’s picture from Oceanography is still on it, and it has gone around since lunch: forty-one comments now, one of them *is this the airport girl??*, and a list of likes long enough that he stops reading it at a name he heard once this morning, in Theo’s voice, under Julian’s birthday dinner: Kenzie Rourke. He reads nothing else on it. He scrolls past, and types *Nora Calloway* into the search box.

body.name: In Memory of Nora Calloway
body.text: Nora Grace Calloway · 1989–2009 · Selma · Marisol · soprano. For everybody who loved her.

body: The wall under it runs in clumps: a flood in April, a trickle all summer, another at All Souls, another at Christmas, then the first of January and nothing since. The first picture is a choir retreat at the Mission in 2008: twenty girls on the steps in white blouses, and one in the second row who has been told to hold still and is not holding still. After it, a girl asleep on a bus with her mouth open, and a caption in somebody’s capitals: SHE WILL KILL ME FOR THIS. After that the same girl at an upright piano in a Santa hat, in the middle of a note, her throat wide open on it. The one after is the Point, the wall in daylight, from behind. A girl in a jean jacket is walking out toward the rail with one arm flung out for balance, and the sea past the rail is very flat and bright, and on the back of the jacket is Our Lady, with her gold rays and the roses at her feet.

body.name: Rosa Calloway
body.text: Feliz año, mija. Te extrañamos en la mesa. Happy New Year, my girl. We miss you at the table.

body: She has written it twice, in Spanish and then in English, as Nonna does with a prayer: once for herself, once for company.

body: He clicks the number, and the members come up in rows of little faces, three hundred and eighty-six of them, Selma and Marisol and a church choir he never heard of. He knows three. Julian Park-Ellis, with a guitar in his profile picture. Priya Raman, in her RA lanyard, not smiling, correctly. Magdalena Broussard, in a thumbnail the size of a stamp, laughing at something past the edge of the frame.

He goes back. The cursor sits on JOIN GROUP. He enlarges the girl on the path until Our Lady comes apart into squares, gold rays and four orange blocks of roses, and through the glass the radio says again that the phones are down.

journal.text: The black bag isn’t on the top shelf in 412 anymore. Her jacket is in four of the pictures on her memorial page.

response: He goes through the album to its end, one picture at a time. The jacket is in four. Tied around her waist on a fairground midway; on a hook by a kitchen door, under a calendar with the Virgin on it; over the back of a chair at a birthday table, with a cake coming in; and on her, at the wall. The bus, the piano and the choir steps don’t have it. He counts the four twice. He clears the browser’s history, a menu and three clicks on this machine, and logs out.
Priya is at the lobby desk when he comes out, in her robe over sweats, with the clipboard against her chest and her eyes on it.
“Costigan. Bed.”

Priya is at the lobby desk when he comes out, in her robe over sweats, with the clipboard against her chest and her eyes on it.
“Costigan. Bed.”
